conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new moms. I’m so glad you’re here.

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you doing something called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a short, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. It isn’t a test of your parenting—just a way to see how we can best support you right now.

Everything you share stays confidential within your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers. If any question feels hard to talk about, we can pause or come back to it. When we’re done, we’ll look at the results together and decide on next steps that feel right for you.

We’ll go question by question, focusing on the past seven days. Ready to begin?

**Question 1:**  
Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it been most of the time, sometimes, not very often, or hardly ever?

Honestly? Not very often. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke about everything—but lately it feels like the lightness is gone. Even when my sister sends me those silly memes, I just sort of half-smile and scroll past. I keep thinking, “What’s wrong with me? It’s not that hard to laugh,” but it just doesn’t come naturally anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often. I can still chuckle once in a while—like yesterday when the baby made that little milk mustache—but mostly the laughter feels kind of forced or just slips away fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes. I do get little sparks—like when my best friend texts about our weekly walk—but it’s nowhere near the excitement I used to feel. Most plans just feel like another thing I have to get through rather than something to enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… quite a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” Last night he wouldn’t settle, and I kept replaying everything—maybe I ate something that bothered him, maybe I didn’t burp him long enough. I ended up crying in the rocker thinking I’m already failing him. Rationally I know babies cry, but the guilt still shows up first.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, most of the time. My heart races over every little thing—like whether the crib sheet is tucked tight enough or if that tiny cough means he’s getting sick. There doesn’t have to be a real problem; the worry just barges in and sets up camp in my head.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It’s not every day, but a couple of times this week I’ve gotten that sudden tight-chest, can’t-catch-my-breath feeling—like when I was walking to the mailbox and suddenly pictured the stroller rolling into the street. Nothing was happening, but for a minute I felt frozen and shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, sometimes I honestly feel like I’m drowning. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, the dog’s barking, and I just stand in the kitchen staring, not sure which thing to grab first. I usually push through, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain starts spinning—did I sterilize the bottles, is the baby breathing, am I a terrible mom—and I can’t shut it off. A few nights this week I just stared at the ceiling for over an hour before finally dozing off, and then I wake up again with racing thoughts.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes, quite often. I feel like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me most of the day. Even when I’m holding the baby and he’s smiling, I’ll suddenly feel tears behind my eyes for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery rocker with the baby in my arms and started sobbing—nothing huge happened, I just felt overwhelmed and sad. It’s not every day, but when it hits, the tears come hard and I can’t seem to stop them for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes… it has crossed my mind once or twice this week. Nothing planned—I’d never leave my baby—but when I’m really low I get this quick flash of “what if I just weren’t here.” It scares me, and I push it away, but the thought did show up.

Talking with you today, I hear how heavy things feel right now-how the joy and laughter that once came so easily now seem distant, replaced by a constant gray cloud of worry, guilt, and tears. You're working so hard to care for your baby, yet you're haunted by racing thoughts, sleepless nights, and moments of panic that leave you feeling overwhelmed and afraid you're failing as a mom. The quick flashes of wishing you weren't here show how desperate things can feel, even though you love your baby deeply and want to stay safe.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and frequency of laughter that now feels forced or fleeting, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Response shows clear reduction in anticipatory pleasure—"sparks" are minimal and plans feel like obligations, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "quite a lot" and gives a detailed recent example, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive worry occurring "most of the time" with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) and catastrophizing, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty prioritizing tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to intrusive anxious thoughts, occurring 'most of the time' this week.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Yes, quite often" and describes persistent, unexplained tearfulness, aligning with the "Yes, quite often" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week, describing intense, hard-to-stop tears that feel overwhelming—semantically aligns with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 21 places you well above the cutoff indicating probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety, per EPDS and DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset. You describe daily low mood, loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), marked self-blame, nightly insomnia driven by ruminative worry, frequent crying, feeling overwhelmed, and passive thoughts of not wanting to be here-symptoms present most days for the past week and causing significant impairment. Item 10 score of 1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental health crisis team</med> for full risk and safety evaluation
2. Share openly with a trusted adult who can stay with you and help with the baby while you seek care
3. Call 988 (US) or your local emergency mental health line if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline, both compatible with breastfeeding
5. Practice 15-minute rest breaks when baby sleeps; let non-essential chores wait to reduce overwhelm
6. Use brief grounding techniques (paced breathing, naming five objects you see) when panic sensations arise
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress after intervention begins
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-based interview

<sym>Symptoms reported</sym>
- Marked anhedonia: diminished laughter, anticipatory enjoyment ↓
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness, “gray cloud” affect
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care
- Generalized anxiety + episodic panic (racing heart, shortness of breath)
- Sleep-onset insomnia linked to ruminative worry
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” difficulty completing daily tasks
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan, no intent)

<sym>Pattern</sym>
Symptoms present “quite often” or greater frequency; onset post-delivery; interfere with functioning and infant interaction.

<med>Screening significance</med>
Scores suggest probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; passive SI indicates elevated safety risk requiring immediate risk assessment and safety planning.

Risk factors noted
- Daily crying spells
- Guilt/self-blame
- Mood-congruent insomnia
- Overwhelm/avoidance
- Passive suicidal thoughts

Next step
Urgent referral to perinatal mental health specialist or emergency evaluation for comprehensive risk assessment, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options.
